The most interesting thing about social trading is that for the first time in years, there’s actual alpha to find on the timeline again.

I’ve come across several calls over the last few weeks that did a clean 5-10x right after, with enough time and liquidity to actually accumulate.

Haven’t felt this since 2019, back before the whole thing turned into an insider game where the moment you saw something on the timeline, you were already exit liquidity.

Feels good to see people winning together again, instead of the endless PvP where it was just about extracting each other.

Never stop scrolling.

make the most of the next few months. these windows are rare.

One optimistic and still very-non-consensus belief I have about the far future of cryptography:

I think that there is a 33% chance that, for average real-world computation, there exist ways to implement all three of what I call the Egyptian God Protocols (SNARK, FHE, iO) with 1+ε factor overhead (meaning, for large enough instances, the added overhead of cryptographizing a computation becomes arbitrarily small compared to the base cost of doing the computation itself)

And a 60% chance that all three can be done with single-digit overhead (ie. <10x, measured in total cost of energy plus amortized compute)

I think there's a good chance we'll get one of these (probably SNARKs with single-digit overhead) by the end of this decade. After all, we're already there for specialized hash functions and for some LLM inference.

Many years of hard work went into the Poseidon family of hashes, and they have provided great real-world value on Ethereum and elsewhere and will continue to do so for several years. They are the reason why it's fast to generate a client-side SNARK for a modern privacy-protocol.

The fact that we have ultra-fast general-purpose STARKs (mid-three-digit overhead for basically any batched computation) and may well soon drop to double-digit or even lower is more amazing than anything that we had been hoping for in the early 2020s.

Big congratulations to all involved in Poseidon, and all involved in STARKs.
 https://t.co/cdERDYkj6n

𝐀𝐌𝐄𝐑𝐈𝐂𝐀 𝐌𝐔𝐒𝐓 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐓𝐑𝐎𝐋 𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐎𝐖𝐍 𝐀𝐈 𝐅𝐔𝐓𝐔𝐑𝐄

America must be very careful.

There is a growing debate about whether building data centers is worth the pressure they place on electricity grids, water supplies, and local communities.

These concerns are legitimate. Every major industrial expansion has costs, and data-center developers should be required to address them honestly. But America must not confuse refusing to build infrastructure with eliminating the demand for it.

If the United States blocks data centers at home, the need for computing power will not disappear. The data centers will simply be built somewhere else. Along with them will go the investment, jobs, technological capacity, and, most importantly, control.

That is not environmental leadership. It is the outsourcing of strategic dependence.

Europe has already shown us the danger of this approach.

For years, much of Europe reduced its domestic energy production while becoming increasingly dependent on imported Russian gas. In 2021, Russia supplied approximately 45% of the European Union’s gas imports.

The arrangement appeared economically rational. Europe received relatively cheap energy while keeping much of the environmental and geopolitical cost conveniently outside its borders.

Then Russia invaded Ukraine.

Europe’s dependence on Russian energy did not, by itself, cause the war. But it gave Russia enormous leverage, restricted Europe’s choices, and may have influenced Putin’s calculation that Europe would hesitate to impose serious consequences.

Energy that Europe had treated as an ordinary commodity suddenly revealed itself as a strategic weapon.

Europe eventually responded. It imposed sanctions, found alternative suppliers, and dramatically reduced its dependence on Russian fuel.

But the adjustment came at an enormous economic cost, after the vulnerability had already been exposed.

The lesson is not that international trade is bad.

The lesson is that a country should think very carefully before placing infrastructure essential to its security in the hands of others.

Artificial intelligence now presents America with a similar strategic choice.

Data centers are not merely large buildings filled with servers. They are becoming the factories of intelligence.

They will power scientific research, military systems, financial markets, medicine, communications, and almost every important industry.

A country that controls computing capacity, reliable energy, and the physical infrastructure connecting them controls an essential part of its future.

This does not mean America should approve every proposed facility or allow companies to ignore local communities.

Data centers should pay appropriately for the power and infrastructure they consume. Developers should invest in additional power generation, transmission, storage, and water-efficient cooling. Local communities should share in the economic benefits rather than simply absorb the costs.

But there is a profound difference between regulating construction responsibly and making construction impossible.

If America chooses the second path merely to make its domestic emissions look lower, it will not make the world cleaner.

It will simply move the emissions and infrastructure elsewhere, potentially to countries with weaker environmental standards, while surrendering the jobs and strategic advantage as well.

A clean national balance sheet can be an accounting illusion when the dirty work has merely been moved abroad.

The atmosphere does not care on which side of a border the electricity was generated.

National security, however, cares deeply about who controls the power, the chips, the networks, and the computing capacity.

The world is not perfect. Every serious decision involves trade-offs.

1/2
